title: The alphabet prayer
hookLine: a man who knows no prayers recites the alphabet and asks God to arrange the letters
tomorrow: the fire, the place, the prayer

lines: THE FEELING, BUT NOT THE WORDS.
cards: You want to write a card to someone who's grieving, and nothing sounds right. You start, delete it, start again. Or you want to apologize, and every sentence comes out wrong.

You have the feeling but not the words. Today's Hasidic story is about a man in exactly that spot, standing before God with a full heart and an empty vocabulary. What he did is so simple it almost sounds like a joke.

teach.h: NO BOOK, NO PRAYERS, ONLY LETTERS.
teach.b: The story is told in many ways. In one telling, a simple Jew, a farmer or a villager, is stuck somewhere on the way when it's time to pray, without his prayer book. He never learned the prayers by heart.
He only knows the letters. So he stands and says the Hebrew alphabet, slowly, one letter after another.
Dalet. All twenty-two. Then he says something like this: Master of the world, I don't know the prayers.
But you know them. Here are all the letters.

Please, you arrange them into the right words. In the Hasidic telling, a great rebbe hears of it, or sees it in a vision, and says this was the finest prayer offered that day. Here's what the story sees.
Every Hebrew prayer is made from those same letters. Psalms, blessings, the Shema: all of it is alef-bet, arranged. The man isn't skipping the prayer.
He's handing over all of it, raw, and trusting the one who hears to put it together. A real line in the daily prayers has the same humility.

teach.h: O LORD, OPEN THOU MY LIPS.
teach.b: Before the central standing prayer, Jews say a verse from the Psalms: "O Lord, open Thou my lips."
Even the most learned begin by admitting they need help to find the words.

how: Before the Amidah, the central standing prayer, Jews quietly say the verse O Lord, open Thou my lips, and many teachers tell the alphabet story to comfort those who don't know the Hebrew prayers.

games.q: it's time to pray. you have no prayer book, and you never learned the words by heart. what do you do?
o: say the alphabet and ask God to arrange it.
make up something that sounds official.
games.why: in the story he said the alphabet, letter by letter, and asked God to arrange them. a rebbe called it the finest prayer of the day.

practice: Think of something you want to say, to God if you pray, or to someone in your life, and can't find the words for. Don't hunt for the words now; just set down the raw pieces one by one, like letters: a name, a feeling, a memory.
If you pray, you can ask for them to be arranged; if not, simply trust that what's true in them will come through.
